subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An ecosystem is best defined as which of the following?
options: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and their non-living environment
A group of the same species living together in one area
Only the physical, non-living parts of an environment
The total number of plant species in a region
questions.explain: An ecosystem is the interaction between biotic (living) organisms and abiotic (non-living) components in an area.

questions.q: Which term describes organisms, such as green plants, that make their own food by photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Producers convert sunlight energy into chemical energy (glucose) through photosynthesis, forming the base of the food chain.

questions.q: Organisms that break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil are called what?
questions.explain: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead matter and recycle nutrients back into the soil.

questions.q: Roughly how much of the energy available at one trophic level is passed on to the next?
questions.explain: Only around 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels, as most is lost as heat, movement and waste.

questions.q: In the nutrient cycle, what are the three main stores of nutrients?
questions.explain: Nutrients cycle between three stores: biomass (living organisms), litter (dead material) and the soil.

questions.q: Why do tropical rainforests recycle nutrients very quickly?
options: Warm, wet conditions speed up the decomposition of dead material
Cold temperatures slow down plant growth
There are very few decomposers in the soil
Nutrients are stored mainly in deep soil layers
questions.explain: High temperatures and rainfall accelerate decomposition, so nutrients are rapidly returned and taken up by dense vegetation.

questions.q: A farmer clears rainforest and the thin soil quickly loses its fertility. The main reason for this is that:
options: Most nutrients were stored in the vegetation, which has been removed
The soil was already very deep and rich in nutrients
Rainfall in the area is extremely low
Decomposition stops completely once trees are cut
questions.explain: In rainforests the largest nutrient store is the biomass, so removing trees strips the system of its nutrients.

questions.q: Tropical rainforests are found mainly in which location?
questions.explain: Tropical rainforests lie in a band around the Equator where it is hot and wet all year.

questions.q: Which of the following is a direct cause of tropical deforestation?
questions.explain: Clearing land for cattle ranching and commercial farming is one of the main direct causes of rainforest loss.

questions.q: Deforestation can increase soil erosion because:
options: Tree roots no longer bind the soil and rain washes it away
Trees add extra weight that compacts the soil
Removing trees increases the number of decomposers
Bare soil absorbs far more water than forested soil
questions.explain: Without roots to hold the soil and a canopy to intercept rain, exposed soil is easily washed away by heavy rainfall.

questions.q: Coral reefs are increasingly threatened by coral bleaching, which is mainly caused by:
questions.explain: Warmer seas cause corals to expel the algae that give them colour and food, leaving them bleached and vulnerable.

questions.q: One global impact of large-scale rainforest deforestation is:
options: Increased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, adding to climate change
A large fall in global sea temperatures
An increase in the size of the ozone layer
A general cooling of the global climate
questions.explain: Rainforests store carbon; removing and burning them releases CO2 and reduces the amount absorbed, enhancing global warming.

questions.q: A conservation group wants to reduce deforestation while still allowing local people to earn a living. Which strategy best achieves this?
options: Clear-felling large areas for cattle ranches
Banning all human activity with no alternative livelihoods
Building new roads deep into the forest
questions.explain: Ecotourism and selective logging provide income while conserving most of the forest, making them more sustainable options.

questions.q: An area where water demand is greater than water supply is said to have a water:
questions.explain: A water deficit occurs where demand exceeds available supply; a surplus is where supply exceeds demand.

questions.q: Economic water scarcity differs from physical water scarcity because it is caused by:
options: A lack of money or infrastructure to access available water
A complete absence of any water in the region
Too much rainfall throughout the year
questions.explain: Economic scarcity means water exists but people cannot afford the wells, pipes or treatment needed to use it.

questions.q: A water transfer scheme is designed to:
options: Move water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit
Reduce the demand for water in cities
questions.explain: Water transfer schemes redistribute water via pipes or canals from regions with plenty to regions that are short of it.

questions.q: A dry region needs to increase its water supply sustainably and at low cost. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Building several very large concrete dams
questions.explain: Low-cost, small-scale methods like rainwater harvesting and efficient irrigation increase supply without high expense or environmental damage.

questions.q: Desertification is best described as:
options: The degradation of land in arid and semi-arid areas, often turning it into desert
The natural expansion of tropical rainforest
The flooding of low-lying coastal land
The permanent freezing of soil in polar regions
questions.explain: Desertification is the process by which fertile land in dry areas becomes increasingly degraded and desert-like.

questions.q: Which combination of factors can cause desertification?
questions.explain: Removing vegetation through overgrazing and over-cultivation, combined with reduced rainfall from climate change, degrades the soil.

questions.q: In the Sahel, farmers build lines of stones (stone bunds or 'magic stones') across their fields mainly to:
options: Trap rainwater and reduce soil erosion
Mark the boundaries of their land
Raise the temperature of the soil
questions.explain: Stone lines slow surface run-off so water soaks in and soil is held in place, helping to combat desertification cheaply.
